Mining · South Africa

Structures in your tailings zones and at your mine boundaries, mapped from the air

A current list of the structures inside the tailings, blast and hazard zones your engineers define, settlement growth at the edge of your mining right, and surface excavation on and around it, compared between dated surveys. Many South African mines already fly their own drones, so we run the analysis on that imagery and use satellite scenes between flights. A person reviews every result.

Talk to us about your drone imagery See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

Zones fixed on paper, land that keeps changing

“What sits inside our tailings zone, and is it growing?”

The zone in your emergency plan was drawn once; the structures inside it change every year. Preparedness, engagement and the plan itself need a current list.

“Settlement keeps creeping up to our boundary.”

Townships and informal settlement grow towards mining-right boundaries, haul roads and rehabilitated land. The edge that matters moves, and a register from two years ago no longer describes it.

“We fly drones every month, and still count by hand.”

The survey team produces orthophotos on a cycle, but turning them into a list of new structures near a zone or boundary is still someone’s spreadsheet.

“We have to show rehabilitation progress.”

Closure plans and audits need dated evidence of revegetation and earthworks, compared between dates and set against a pre-disturbance baseline.

Who this is for

  • Tailings engineers and engineers of record
  • Emergency-preparedness managers
  • Mine land and property managers
  • Social-performance and community-relations teams
  • Closure, rehabilitation and environmental managers
  • Mine surveyors and geomatics teams, as users
  • Sustainability and ESG reporting teams

Tailings, blast and hazard zones

A current list of the structures inside your zones

You supply the zones: the inundation area from a dam-break study, a blast exclusion radius, a flood line or a safety setback. We list each structure the review confirms inside them, with its location, its distance to the source and its band, and show how settlement inside each zone changes between surveys. Where villages are dense or roofs are hard to read, reviewers mark structures by hand on high-resolution imagery.

On request, we add estimated households derived from the structure counts, with the assumptions stated, for preparedness planning and engagement, and screen the zones for historically flooded and low-lying ground. Zones are re-surveyed on the schedule you agree with us, with a notice after each survey saying what changed.

The Department of Water and Sanitation has called on mines to register their tailings dams on its dam-safety database (DWS). A current list of the structures inside the downstream zone belongs with that record: it describes the zone as it is today, not as it was when the study was done.

What you receive

  • A register of structures inside each zone, with distance to the source
  • Settlement growth inside each zone between surveys
  • Estimated households with stated assumptions, on request
  • Flood-exposure screening of the zones
  • A change notice after each re-survey
  • A PDF report and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers

What this register is, and isn’t

It is a list of structures in the zones you define, with the imagery date on every record. It is not a dam-break model, a dam-safety assessment or a statement of conformance with any tailings standard, and it counts structures, not people at risk.

Your drone imagery, our analysis

Get more from the drone imagery you already fly

Mining houses are well represented on SACAA’s list of UAS operators (SACAA): many South African mines fly their own drones under their own operator certificates. The flying is done; the analysis often is not.

Send the orthophotos or GeoTIFFs your survey team already produces. We run the structure register, the zone and boundary analysis and the change detection on them, have a person review every result, and return the register and GIS layers in the formats your GIS team uses. Between flights, or over the parts of the right you do not fly, dated satellite scenes show what changed where they exist.

Where you want new drone surveys, they are subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires, including approvals for flights within 50 m of structures, people or public roads and the landowner’s permission for every flight.

Analysis of your own imagery

  • Orthophotos and GeoTIFFs from your own flights
  • The same register, zone and change layers as our own surveys
  • Satellite scenes between flights
  • A sample checked first, because results depend on the imagery’s resolution and quality

Imagery: yours, archive or new capture

Mining-right boundaries

What stands inside your right, and in a ring around it

Mining rights are granted under the Mineral and Petroleum Resources Development Act, and their edges are where land pressure shows first. We list the structures inside your boundary and in a ring around it, map new structures, cleared ground and tracks at the boundary between dates, and produce a structure layer across the whole right for your land team. On drone imagery, a reviewer checks fence lines and gates; fences are too thin to find automatically on satellite imagery.

We work from the boundary you give us and do not verify title, tenure or surface rights. A boundary that needs surveying or beaconing is a professional land surveyor’s work.

Surface excavation

Pits, spoil and disturbed ground on and around your right

New pits, spoil heaps, water-filled excavations and disturbed ground inside and around your right are mapped from dated imagery, with new sites flagged between dates and confirmed by a reviewer. In the rainy season, radar comparisons show larger ground changes even under cloud, and flagged areas are followed up with optical imagery or a drone check.

What we map is the ground. We do not identify, count or follow people, and underground workings and covered shafts are not visible from above. Alerts are indications for your teams to check, not proof of anything, and whether and how to act on them is your decision.

POPIA

If you plan to use a register of surface activity as evidence about unlawful conduct, POPIA’s prior-authorisation rule (s57) may apply to your organisation. Take advice before you decide how a register will be used.

POPIA and aerial imagery

Expansions and resettlement

Record the footprint before the census

When a pit, dump or tailings facility expands, we produce a dated record of the structures inside the new footprint, with reviewer categories such as main building, outbuilding, livestock enclosure or under construction, and on request estimated households. South Africa has no single national resettlement regulation, so the process follows the project’s own resettlement plan and, where DFIs or Equator Principles banks are involved, IFC Performance Standard 5. Our dated record supports the census and asset inventory and the cut-off-date records; it does not replace them, and categories do not establish use, ownership or value.

Resettlement cut-off-date baselines

Rehabilitation and closure

Dated evidence of revegetation and earthworks

Revegetation trends

Vegetation cover on rehabilitated land compared between dates, from Copernicus Sentinel data and, where flown, drone elevation models. It shows the trend; it is not an ecological assessment or a closure sign-off.

Earthworks and volumes

Cut and fill between drone visits, and stockpile and void volumes from drone elevation models, to support your mine surveyors. Not a statutory survey.

A pre-disturbance baseline

A land-use and land-cover baseline for new ground before it is disturbed, and the imagery history of what was there before.

Financial provision for rehabilitation and closure is made under the NEMA Financial Provisioning Regulations, 2015, and the compliance date for holders of mining rights has been extended pending amendments (statement). Dated evidence of rehabilitation supports those assessments; it does not calculate the provision.

How it works

From zone file to reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the zone and boundary files, tell us what you already fly and what the register is for. We agree the zones, imagery and deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Analyse your imagery

    Your orthophotos, or dated satellite scenes and open building datasets, give the first structure register for every zone and boundary.

  3. Fill the gaps

    Satellite scenes between your flights, and drone surveys where you want them, subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires.

  4. Review and deliver

    A person checks every result before the report and GIS layers go to the contacts you name. Re-surveys follow the schedule you set.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map structures, excavations, tracks and cleared ground visible from the air
  • List structures inside the zones your engineers define, with distances
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Analyse the drone imagery you already fly

What we don’t do

  • Model dam breaks, blasts or floods, or assess dam safety
  • Identify, count or follow people
  • See underground workings, or verify title and tenure
  • Certify volumes or calculate financial provision

Frequently asked questions

Do you model dam breaks or blast zones?

No. Your engineers supply the zones, from the dam-break study, the blast design or your emergency plan. We list the structures inside them, each with its location and distance to the source, and show how settlement inside them changes between surveys.

Can you tell us how many people live in the zone?

We report structures, and on request estimated households derived from them, with the assumptions stated in the report. Estimates support preparedness planning; they are not a census and never replace the engagement your emergency plan requires.

We already fly our own drones. Can you use our imagery?

Yes. Send the orthophotos or GeoTIFFs your survey team already produces and we run the same structure, change and boundary analysis on them, with a reviewer confirming every result. Results depend on the imagery’s resolution and quality, which we check on a sample first.

Can you tell us who is digging on our right?

No. We map the ground, such as pits, spoil heaps, water-filled excavations and disturbed ground, with new sites flagged between dates and confirmed by a reviewer. We never identify or count people, and underground workings are not visible from above.

Can your baseline replace our resettlement census?

No. A dated record of the structures in an expansion footprint supports your census and asset inventory and, where lenders apply it, the IFC Performance Standard 5 cut-off-date records. Categories describe what the imagery shows; compensation needs ground verification.

Can your stockpile volumes stand as a statutory survey?

No. Volumes from drone elevation models support your mine surveyors; they are not a statutory survey, and we do not publish tolerance figures.

Can you confirm our mining-right boundary?

No. We work from the boundary you give us and do not verify title or tenure. Where a boundary needs to be surveyed or beaconed, that is the work of a professional land surveyor.

Talk to us about your own drone imagery

Tell us what you already fly, how often and in what format, and send the zone or boundary files (Shapefile, GeoPackage, KML or GeoJSON). We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
